reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: A highly lethal herbicide with no effective antidote; even small deliberate ingestions of concentrated solution are frequently fatal
It concentrates in and selectively destroys the lungs, causing progressive pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage, and then relentless fibrosis over days to weeks
Early features include painful corrosive burns to the mouth, throat, and oesophagus, vomiting, and abdominal pain
Oxygen supplementation should generally be avoided or minimised, as high oxygen tension accelerates free-radical lung injury; supplemental oxygen is reserved for severe, refractory hypoxaemia
Immediate gastrointestinal decontamination with an adsorbent such as activated charcoal or Fuller's earth is a priority if the patient presents very early
Enhanced elimination (haemoperfusion or haemodialysis) and immunosuppression with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide have been tried, but none reliably alters the poor outcome
Acute kidney injury and hepatic injury commonly precede the delayed, usually fatal, pulmonary fibrosis
Plasma paraquat concentration plotted against time since ingestion helps estimate prognosis and guide the intensity of intervention
reference.pathophysiology: Paraquat undergoes cyclical reduction and oxidation (redox cycling), generating large amounts of superoxide and other reactive oxygen species that deplete NADPH and cause lipid peroxidation and cell death. It is actively taken up and concentrated by alveolar epithelial (type I and II) cells, making the lung the primary target: an early destructive phase of alveolitis and haemorrhagic oedema is followed by an obliterative pulmonary fibrosis. The kidneys and liver, which also accumulate the compound, sustain acute injury, and high oxygen tensions worsen the oxidative damage.
additionalDifferentials: Other lethal pesticide ingestions (organophosphate, aluminium phosphide)
Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Plasma or urine paraquat level and the urine dithionite qualitative test
Serial renal and liver function tests
Arterial blood gas and serial chest imaging to track evolving lung injury
Prognostic assessment using plasma concentration versus time since ingestion
redFlags: Ingestion of concentrated solution or any large deliberate ingestion
Early acute kidney injury, which predicts high toxin burden and poor outcome
Progressive hypoxaemia and radiographic lung changes
Extensive oropharyngeal and oesophageal corrosive burns
Rising plasma paraquat level for the time since ingestion indicating a lethal exposure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor and dose-dependent; ingestion of concentrated formulation is usually fatal, with death from multi-organ failure early or from progressive pulmonary fibrosis over subsequent days to weeks, and no treatment has been shown to reliably improve survival.
pitfalls: Giving liberal supplemental oxygen, which accelerates oxidative lung injury
Delaying adsorbent decontamination in an early presentation
Offering false reassurance during the deceptively stable early period before lung failure
Underestimating lethality and under-treating the psychosocial and palliative needs of the patient
